title: Ashtpadi 18, salok: the True Guru
hook: the salok honors the True Guru (Sukhmani 18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 17, sachiaaraa, and your line: truth lived. Did you do one true thing instead of arguing for one? Today the eighteenth ashtpadi begins, and it's about the one who teaches truth. Day five hundred six.

A third-grade teacher catches a kid drawing in the margins and, instead of a scolding, hands over a sketchbook. A coach says one sentence at the right moment. A grandmother teaches bread and, without saying so, patience. Some of those teachers never hear what they did. The word Sikh itself is about exactly this relationship. And the salok of the eighteenth ashtpadi is about the teacher at its center. Today: the True Guru.
screen: `A TEACHER WHO CHANGED YOU.` → `A SKETCHBOOK. ONE SENTENCE. BREAD.` → `SOME NEVER HEAR WHAT THEY DID.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: the one who knows the True Being is called the True Guru. In his company the Sikh is carried across; Nanak, sing the praises of the Lord. Start with one word in it: Sikh. It's traced to a Sanskrit word for a student, a learner, a disciple. A Sikh, at root, is someone who is learning. Not someone who has finished. Which means every Sikh is defined by a relationship: you can't be a learner without a teacher. Then satgur, the True Guru. Notice how the salok defines it. Not by title, not by miracle, not by birth. By knowing: the one who knows the True Being, sat purakh, is the True Guru. Sikhs understand the True Guru in more than one way, and they hold these together. God is the True Guru, the first and final teacher. The ten Gurus, from Guru Nanak to Guru Gobind Singh, are honored as the True Guru, one light in ten lives. And tradition says Guru Gobind Singh passed the Guruship to the Guru Granth Sahib itself, the scripture, honored as the living Guru, and the community of the Khalsa is called the Guru Panth. When this salok says in his company, Sikhs today hear the sangat gathered around the Guru Granth Sahib. Then the last phrase: sing the praises. The response to having a true teacher isn't to admire the teacher from a distance. It's to sing: to turn the gratitude outward, toward the One the teacher points to. That's the pattern of the next few days. The Guru cares for the Sikh. The Sikh serves. And the line runs both ways.
screen: `SIKH: A LEARNER.` · `SATGUR: THE ONE WHO KNOWS THE TRUE.` · `GOD, TEN GURUS, THE GRANTH.` · `IN HIS COMPANY, SING.` · then, large: `THANK THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a teacher. Bring one to mind: a schoolteacher, a mentor, a parent, an author, anyone who taught you something true. See their face, or their handwriting, or the room where you learned from them. Remember one specific thing they gave you. Then thank them, silently, in plain words. If they're still living, notice whether you could send that thank-you for real today. If you pray, thank the One they pointed you toward. The bell holds the time.
Satgur, the True Guru. The salok: the one who knows the True Being is the satgur, and in that company the Sikh, the learner, is carried across.
Your line: thank the teacher. Today, send one real thank-you to someone who taught you something, and name the thing. Day five hundred six.

screen: `DAY 506 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE GURU CHERISHES THE SIKH.`

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the eighteenth ashtpadi with the salok on the True Guru; Sikhs honor God, the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib as Guru, and gather as sangat in its presence.

fork.setup: you've found a true teacher. by the eighteenth salok, what's the response?
options: admire the teacher from a distance.
sing the praises of the One the teacher points to.
become a teacher yourself right away.
fork.reveal: the salok ends: Nanak, sing the praises of the Lord. gratitude to the teacher turns outward, toward the One.

original.note: Gurmukhi: satgur, the True Guru; sat, true, and gur, teacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sikh is just the name of a religion.
what it means: a Sikh is a learner, defined by a relationship with the True Guru.

what a scholar hears: Sikh derives from Sanskrit shishya, disciple; the salok defines satgur as the one who knows sat purakh, and tradition dates the passing of Guruship to the Granth and Panth to 1708.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 18, salok (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286)

notes: Salok of ashtpadi 18 paraphrased: sat purakh jin jaaniaa satgur tis kaa naau; tis kai sang sikh udharai Nanak har gun gaau. Confirm Ang 286.
Sikh from Sanskrit shishya: standard derivation; confirm.
Guruship passing to the Guru Granth Sahib and Guru Panth in 1708: confirm framing.
